qualitative_review: [R01] This is the only remaining idea that attacks the validity rather than the repeatability of the 14-slot vocabulary, and the vocabulary is the single assumption every other audit in the round is conditioned on. The design is textbook-on-purpose and honest about its circularity: the same analyst wrote the glosses and applied the labels, so lexical recovery is a weak but non-zero external check, and the S6/S9 branch prediction is a genuine out-of-sample re-test of finding 2. Reusing 225 frozen rows on CPU makes it the cheapest high-stakes test in the set. Its weakest link is that a null ARI is confounded with 'the glosses simply do not carry lexical signal', and no positive control on lexical discriminability is proposed. | [R02] This turns the atlas's least-examined assumption - that the 14 slots are discovered rather than imposed - into a falsifiable test using only frozen rows, and the pre-registered prediction that S6 and S9 separate into unsown branches gives it a second bite that the coding could not inherit. The design also states the right disconfirmations (null at every k; stable structure only far below k=14), so both tails carry information about the headline deep-grammar claim. The central weakness is same-source circularity: gloss_en was written by the analyst who assigned slot, so high ARI shows the labels are lexically grounded, not that the grammar is real, and this can only be flagged as a sensitivity. Cheap, CPU-only, and it directly tests findings 1-2. | [R03] This is the clearest statement in the wave of a question the repo has never actually asked: whether the 14 slots are recovered by the data or imposed by the codebook. The shift from reliability to validity is well argued, and the free re-test of the S6/S9 split by a route that cannot inherit the fork is a genuine bonus. The main weakness is that the outcome is semi-predictable: glosses are analyst-written and semantically close to the slot names, so a middling ARI above nulls is the likely result and would be read either way. | [R04] The reliability-to-validity pivot is the right framing and the design is unusually clean: frozen vocabulary, frozen preprocessing, fixed-margin nulls, and a reported k-curve rather than one tuned number. But the strongest form of the critique is only partly answered, because the same analyst wrote the glosses and the slot labels, so lexical recovery above chance is as consistent with gloss-writing habits as with a real deep grammar; that circularity is acknowledged but not removed. Its most valuable by-product is the free out-of-sample look at the S6/S9 split, and even a null is interpretable as the vocabulary being imposed rather than induced. Scope is internal to the atlas, so it adds no traditions.
uncertainties: [R01] I am unsure whether 225 short, multilingual, partly duplicated gloss strings carry enough signal for any clustering to be interpretable at all, which is why rigor is not higher. Whether a strong positive result would survive the same-source circularity objection is also unclear, since terminology overlap and functional overlap are not separated. | [R02] I am unsure whether the expected outcome is decisive: 'above null but imperfect' is the most likely result and is hard to interpret, so the most informative scenario may be the least probable. The frozen k grid and preprocessing choices also determine how much of the forking-paths critique survives the freeze, and I cannot tell from the text how much of the reported uncertainty will be about the vocabulary versus the clustering. | [R03] Whether 225 short, partly duplicated bilingual glosses carry enough signal for a stable 14-way partition versus a coarser trunk is unknown; the repo's own clustering already collapses to one trunk on presence data. I am also unsure whether any ARI value could be interpreted cleanly given that the same author wrote glosses and labels, even with the declared sensitivity. | [R04] I am unsure how much credit to give a test whose likely positive result is difficult to interpret (gloss circularity) yet whose negative result is very informative. Feasibility could be even cheaper than assumed if a standard clustering stack is used unchanged.

qualitative_review: [R01] Scoping re-coding to the mechanically enumerable flip-distance-1 cells is the right economy: a random kappa sample spends effort on cells no claim depends on. The per-claim decidable/undecidable verdict before any null model is run is exactly the sequencing the round needs, and it directly targets the perfect complementarity/implication rules named in findings. The weakness is that a sole coder adjudicating against sources is still one coder, so 'adjudicated error' is a floor with unknown bias, not a measure of error. | [R02] Well targeted: because perfect rules have flip-distance 1, the claim set rests on an enumerable handful of cells, and adjudicating exactly those against sources/ uses an external criterion rather than another agreement statistic. The predicted split into 'survives on the strong-primary subset' and 'undecidable without re-coding' would give a per-claim verdict that any later audit needs, and it is pre-registered against a frozen codebook. The week-one framing is optimistic - per-cell source adjudication across ~60 texts plus a washout re-code is more like three to four weeks - and with a sole coder the surviving-error bound will be wide. Its value is concentrated in the possibility that one flipped cell retires a headline rule. | [R03] Scoping re-coding to the cells a claim actually depends on is a real methodological improvement over uniform kappa sampling, and it is the only idea here that returns a per-claim decidable/undecidable verdict rather than another statistic. The gain is diagnostic rather than substantive: it tells you which findings survive measurement error, not what documents do. Feasibility depends on how many load-bearing cells have primary text in sources/, which the sources table suggests may be well under all of them. | [R04] Scoping re-coding to the mechanically enumerable load-bearing set converts an unfocused reliability exercise into a decision about which claims are decidable, and the per-claim verdict arrives before any null or interval is computed. The methods are deliberately textbook (propagation, tier restriction) but the scoping is the contribution and it fits the repo's gate discipline almost perfectly: mechanical cell enumeration, frozen codebook, external criterion in sources/, washout test-retest, and a stated disconfirmation with an error interval. Feasibility is high but not free, since adjudicating cells against primary texts in Cyrillic, Arabic, Han and Thai is slow single-coder work, and cells with no retrievable primary source stay permanently unadjudicable. The information gain is real but partly predictable: P2 essentially anticipates P07-5's tier result at cell granularity.
uncertainties: [R01] I cannot tell from the text how many load-bearing cells lack primary grounding in sources/, which determines whether most rules come back 'undecidable' rather than decided. The predicted 'at least one rule flips' is plausible but not sharply derivable in advance. | [R02] I do not know how many load-bearing cells actually have primary grounding in sources/, and if a large share are unadjudicable the study yields a map of ignorance rather than a decision. Test-retest after washout as the only human reliability number is inherently weak, so the non-trivial-error conclusion may be softer than the decidable/undecidable labels suggest. | [R03] I am uncertain about the one-week estimate: enumerating load-bearing sets for every perfect rule and adjudicating tens of cells against extracted texts with a sole coder reads more like three or four weeks. Whether enough load-bearing cells are primary-grounded to make the verdicts non-trivial is also unresolved. | [R04] Whether sources/ actually grounds enough load-bearing cells is the pivotal unknown; if coverage is thin, the study yields verdicts of undecidable rather than knowledge about documents. I could see feasibility at 3 if the primary texts turn out to be mostly secondary or translated.

qualitative_review: [R01] This is the only idea in the wave that takes the atlas's headline fork out of sample, and it does so with a located directional prediction (diplomatics, ferman, letters patent combine address and recital) rather than a neutral test. Sequential cheapest-bin-first with early stopping and a threshold frozen before coding is the correct asymmetric-falsification logic, and the document-level unit answers P02-2's aggregation critique at the same time. It is also the only idea that de-centres the metropolitan axis materially, adding pre-modern chancery and Ottoman/Indian materials. The costs are real: 30 licence-clear specimens per bin across several traditions and scripts is a heavy solo retrieval and translation burden, and the translation layer remains a live alternative explanation. | [R02] This is the only idea in the set that buys new documents and a genuine out-of-sample test of the S6/S9 fork, and sequential cheapest-falsifying-bin-first is the right ordering for an asymmetrically falsifiable claim. The bin A prediction is directional rather than decorative - diplomatics evidence says pre-modern instruments combine address and recital - so either outcome moves belief about whether the fork is universal or an artefact of modern codified genre separation. Coverage is the best here: pre-modern chancery across several traditions plus South Asian deliberative notes is a real widening beyond the 28-system core. The binding constraint is cost: three sourcing campaigns at >=30 licence-clear specimens each is a retrieval project, not a five-week study. | [R03] This is the only idea in the set that generates evidence the existing corpus cannot generate, and it targets the single most load-bearing claim (S6 perpendicular to S9) with a directional prediction rather than a neutral re-test. The sequential cheapest-bin-first structure with a frozen stopping threshold is exactly the kind of asymmetric falsification design a universal claim invites, and a survival in bin A would be worth more than any internal audit can produce. Its cost is real: three retrieval bins, translation confounds, and single-coder expectation bias on the very cell being sought. | [R04] This is the only idea in the set that takes a headline universal claim out of sample, and the cheapest-bin-first sequencing is the correct asymmetry for a complementarity claim that one co-occurrence can falsify. The directional prior from diplomatics, ferman and letters patent makes bin A a genuine pre-registered prediction rather than a fishing trip, and a falsification would re-scope the fork to modern codified genres, which is a visible belief shift. It is also the broadest item here, opening pre-modern chancery and non-European deliberative material. The cost is real: three bins at 30-plus licence-clear multilingual specimens each, with coding, transcription and translation-layer auditing, is well beyond a modest collection for one person.
uncertainties: [R01] Feasibility is the score I am least sure of: if reliable translations exist in digitised public-domain archives this could be a 3, but a single researcher without reading competence across the relevant scripts may not reach 30 specimens per bin within the window. Rigor is also bounded by sole-coder expectation bias and by co-occurrence living in translators' conventions rather than in the instruments. | [R02] I doubt the one-week-per-bin retrieval assumption, especially for bin B (openly posted French and Indian internal notes) and for bin A in sufficient script/genre variety. The translation-layer confound is the deepest threat: co-occurrence could be a translator's convention, and the proposed fixes (recording translation source as an exclusion) mitigate but do not resolve it. | [R03] Whether bin A can actually yield around 30 licence-clear pre-modern specimens at document level, with usable translations, within a week is the crux and I cannot verify it. The translation-layer alternative (co-occurrence living in translators' conventions) may survive every mitigation and leave the falsification ambiguous. | [R04] Feasibility is the live uncertainty: early stopping means bin A alone may suffice, so an optimistic reading could reach 3, but bin B and C sourcing looks fragile. The translation confound and single-coder expectation bias at exactly the sought cell are only partly handled.

qualitative_review: [R01] Attaching a positive control and a document-absent floor to the finding-5 instrument, before any participant is spent, is exactly the right pre-data move, and the existing harness makes it a few dollars of compute. It correctly identifies that the printed 'no detectable register effect' is currently an unfalsifiable comfort statement at ceiling. The design's own admission is also its limit: a corruption control demonstrates dynamic range for gross damage, which is necessary but not sufficient for a subtle register-shaped effect, so a pass may license an interpretation the control cannot support. | [R02] This supplies a failure condition for an equivalence verdict that currently has none, and it runs pre-recruitment so no participants are spent on an instrument of unknown sensitivity - both clearly right. It is also the cheapest idea in the set, reusing machine_arm.py and the v2 stimuli at demonstrated cost. The weakness is inferential reach: a corruption control proves sensitivity to gross damage, not to a subtle register-shaped cost, so a passing gate licenses a weaker reading than the rule asserts, and the author concedes this rather than solving it. With the human arm paused, the near-term payoff is mostly how the already-printed machine null gets worded. | [R03] As a governance move this is the strongest idea in the wave: it attaches a pre-committed failure condition to an equivalence claim that currently rests on simulation, and it runs before participants are spent. The intellectual yield is bounded, though, because a passed or failed gate changes the interpretation of one null rather than resolving a question about documents. The 'sufficient not necessary' scoping of the corruption control is a good faith attempt at the obvious objection without fully answering it. | [R04] This is the cheapest item in the wave and it protects against a specific, already-printed error: an equivalence verdict produced by instrument blindness rather than by the absence of a register effect. A positive control with a guaranteed SESOI-sized effect plus a document-absent floor, run on the frozen machine panel at roughly three cents a run, gives the TOST branch a pre-committed failure condition and forces the README v1.1/v1.2 null to be either earned or downgraded. Its information value is diagnostic rather than substantive - it decides whether finding 5 means anything - but that is exactly the kind of belief discrimination the criterion rewards. The main conceptual risk is the rubber stamp: a corruption control demonstrates gross-damage sensitivity, which is necessary but not sufficient for a subtle register-shaped effect, and the authors' scope caveat does not fully dissolve that.
uncertainties: [R01] I am unsure whether the gate can be made register-shaped rather than damage-shaped without new item development, which would push feasibility down. Information gain is capped because the gate cannot settle the register question itself, only whether the null is reportable. | [R02] I expect the gate to fail on the near-ceiling half of the panel, which is informative but makes the outcome fairly predictable from v1/v2 ceiling data. Whether the document-absent floor control can be made clean on the same items is unclear to me, and a floor that fires would leave the gate inconclusive rather than failed. | [R03] Whether a gross corruption contrast can establish sensitivity to a subtle register effect at 10 pp is the unresolved validity question, and I doubt the pre-registered scope caveat neutralises it. Feasibility could also be constrained if item variants require touching frozen v2 stimuli during the paused collection window. | [R04] The outcome is fairly predictable from v1 and v2 ceiling patterns, which caps the information gain; a gate that most likely fails is valuable as a stop but not as discovery. I also cannot verify from the text alone whether item variants can be built without touching frozen stimuli during collection.

qualitative_review: [R01] This is the cleanest statement in the set of what would make an absence claim falsifiable: bounds on the 24 off-vocabulary rows plus a slot-blind extraction pass, with the verdict 'vocabulary-conditional' pre-declared. It identifies a concrete structural fact (the recompute filter admits only ^S\d+- rows, so 24 rows in 15 systems enter no published figure) and shows that some headline evidence lives in exactly those rows. The two-stage design with a pre-registered unmappable-rate threshold and a recall floor is the most disciplined gate in the wave. Cost sits in the open-extraction pass, which is real multilingual coding work, not a script. | [R02] This points at a concrete and verifiable mechanical defect: 24 rows (10.7%) sit outside the ^(S\d+)- filter that recompute.py applies, so they enter no census, similarity or clustering figure, while morphology.md asserts full vocabulary coverage - and headline 4's evidence lives in exactly those dropped rows. The bounds pass is cheap and could move presence bits in the thin, mixed systems that carry the absence claims; the open-extraction pass is the expensive and subjective half. Its strongest feature is that both outcomes are pre-specified and informative: a headline moving inside the bounds is a real finding, and a clean collapse plus sub-threshold residue is the vocabularly's first positive test. | [R03] The observation that the recompute filter admits only S-prefixed rows, so 24 rows in 15 systems enter no derived figure, is a concrete and checkable defect rather than a hypothetical, and it bears directly on the strongest absence claims in the atlas. Framing the outcome as vocabulary-conditional reporting rather than a pass/fail verdict is disciplined and keeps the honest null informative. The bounds stage is fairly predictable; the open-extraction stage is where the real information sits and also where single-coder subjectivity is worst. | [R04] This attacks the one conditioning assumption nothing else in the set touches: the pipeline filters to rows matching the canonical slot prefix, so 24 off-vocabulary rows in 15 of 28 systems enter no census, similarity or clustering figure, and at least one README headline rests on rows the census drops. Making absence claims either survive a bounds pass or be relabelled vocabulary-conditional is a clean, pre-registerable and genuinely falsifiable move, and the open-extraction arm with the slot list withheld is the only design here that can surface elements never entered at all. The weak point is single-coder element granularity, which re-enters upstream of every downstream reliability study; the frozen rulebook and per-script recall floor mitigate but do not remove it. Breadth is limited because the corpus is the same 28 systems.
uncertainties: [R01] The bounds stage may be so wide that most claims come back unidentifiable, which the design accepts but which reduces decision value. Element granularity in the open pass is single-coder and could drift upstream of every downstream count, and the 5%/10% thresholds are judgement calls even when frozen. | [R02] Element granularity in five scripts is the weak joint - 'what counts as one requisite' is subjective upstream of every downstream count - and a failed recall floor would leave the open pass uninterpretable. I also cannot tell in advance whether the pre-registered bounds will be too wide to be informative, in which case the disciplined output is 'unidentifiable' rather than a verdict. | [R03] The open-extraction pass depends on a defensible definition of 'one element' across five scripts with one coder and a delayed double pass, and I am not confident that the 5%/10% thresholds can be applied consistently across script strata of very unequal size. I also cannot tell whether the bounds stage alone will already settle most headline claims, making the second stage redundant. | [R04] Whether the bounds turn out wide enough to be uninformative is the main risk, and the authors' own fallback ('unidentifiable from frozen data') is honest but yields less. I am also unsure how much of the open-extraction pass survives in scripts where the extracted text is noisy.

qualitative_review: [R01] Counting analytic degrees of freedom in one registered space rather than running four audits with four p-values is the correct response to the evidence wave's 'methods are never new' finding, and the embedded holdout prediction is a real calibration check. The predicted outcome, however, is close to what the repo already suggests (fork robust to tier and denominator, fragile under tradition blocking), so most of the value is in the audit trail rather than in new belief. At n = 25-28 many nominal specifications will be degenerate duplicates, which inflates robustness mass in a way the design flags but does not solve. | [R02] Consolidating four audits into one registered specification space with a pre-committed holdout is the right shape, and counting analytic degrees of freedom is a genuine improvement over four separate p-values. But the substantive content is largely aggregative: the predicted pattern (fork holds under tier and denominator, weakens under tradition blocking) follows closely from the repo as it stands, so the curve mostly certifies robustness rather than discriminating between explanations. Feasibility is good because the component analyses already exist, though merging them under one written enumeration rule is real engineering with the degenerate-specification trap the author himself names. The holdout prediction is what keeps it from being pure bookkeeping. | [R03] Consolidating four audits into one enumerated specification space with a pre-committed holdout is administratively attractive and would give each headline claim a single auditable number. The risk is that the substantive conclusion is nearly fixed in advance: the fork and stem survive tier and denominator specs, the thin claims do not, which is close to what the repo already says. Counting degrees of freedom is a discipline gain more than a knowledge gain. | [R04] Merging four separate audits into one registered specification space with a rule-enumerated spec set and a pre-committed holdout score is the right way to stop four p-values from being read as four findings, and the rigor is exemplary: enumeration rule, code hash, seed and scoring all frozen before execution. The contribution is bookkeeping of analytic degrees of freedom rather than a new question about documents, so its information gain depends heavily on the masses actually discriminating, which at n = 25-28 with many degenerate duplicates is doubtful. The embedded leave-one-tranche-out prediction is the part most likely to produce genuinely new knowledge. No new traditions are touched.
uncertainties: [R01] The main unresolved question is whether 'robustness mass' can be made a discriminating quantity at this n, or whether it will sit near 1 or near 0 for every claim. The enumeration rule and the codability denominator must be frozen tightly or the multiverse relocates the forking paths. | [R02] With n = 25-28 systems I cannot tell how many nominally distinct specifications will be effective duplicates, and if most collapse the robustness mass is close to uninformative. I am also unclear whether the tradition-blocked specifications will be treated as a separate family or folded into the same mass, which materially changes what a high mass would mean. | [R03] With n = 25-28 systems, many nominal specifications will be near-duplicates, so robustness mass may be an artefact of degenerate enumeration rather than evidence of robustness; I cannot judge from the text how this is prevented. It is also unclear how much of the remaining work is genuinely open given the six-cell curve already built for one family. | [R04] If most specifications collapse to the same handful of partitions, robustness mass will sit near 1 and the study's discriminating power evaporates; the authors flag this but it is the modal outcome I expect. Residual specification space for the three unmerged families also remains unspecified.

qualitative_review: [R01] Asking why the stem is universal rather than only whether it is real is a genuine gap in the round, and the obligation column is the one frozen variable that encodes a mechanism. But the predictor and the outcome were coded by the same analyst from the same rows, so a positive leave-one-system-out result is close to definitional and leave-one-out does not remove that. The obligation-weighted prevalence reordering and the mandate-level fork test are the parts most likely to yield something not already implied by the coding table. Net: a real mechanism question yielding a largely predictable answer. | [R02] This is the only mechanism question in the wave and it targets findings 1-2 rather than re-auditing their statistics, which is a real gap. But the predictor is close to definitional: a slot is present largely because a mandatory requisite was coded in it, so mandate share beating a prevalence-only baseline mostly demonstrates coding regularity, and the leave-one-system-out scoring limits rather than removes that. The mandatory-only re-derivation is already run, and what remains (LOO predictor, obligation-weighted ordering, mandate-level fork test) is days of work on frozen rows. The mandate-level fork test is the most interesting piece and also the thinnest, resting on 11 S6 rows and 3 S9 rows. | [R03] Asking why the stem converges rather than whether it does is the right kind of question, and obligation is genuinely the only frozen variable with mechanistic content. But the design's own weakest point is structural: mandate share and presence are coded from the same rows, so the leave-one-out predictor is close to a noisy re-expression of prevalence and the expected gain over the prevalence baseline is small. The obligation-weighted ordering and the mandate-level fork test are the parts most likely to produce something non-obvious; the LOO predictor is the part least likely to. | [R04] This is the only shortlisted idea that asks why documents converge rather than whether a pattern is real, and it targets findings 1 and 2 with a mechanism the repo already codes but has never used as an explanatory variable. The remaining work (leave-one-system-out mandate-share prediction, obligation-weighted ordering, mandate-level fork test) is arithmetic on frozen data, so it is the cheapest high-synergy item in the set. The problem is that obligation and presence were coded together from the same rows, so a positive result is partly definitional; leave-one-system-out limits but does not separate that alternative, and with 150/225 mandatory rows the predictor has little contrast at slot level n = 14. A null would still be informative, redirecting the universality claim toward functional or conventional accounts.
uncertainties: [R01] I am genuinely torn between 2 and 4 on information gain: the reweighted ordering could demote S7/S13 informatively, but the headline predictor test may be uninterpretable either way. Common-source bias is the main threat and I do not see a clean design fix within frozen data. | [R02] I cannot judge from the text whether the residual (non-definitional) variance is large enough for the LOO comparison to be diagnostic; if it is not, the headline result is predetermined. The obligation column is also analyst-assigned and single-coder, so the 'normative force' mechanism may be an artefact of how mandates were entered - acknowledged, but it bounds how far the result can travel. | [R03] I cannot tell from the text whether mandate share at 24 systems x 14 slots leaves enough between-system contrast for log-loss/AUC to discriminate at all. The bigger doubt is whether any positive result could be distinguished from definitional overlap between the obligation and presence columns. | [R04] The partially-executed mandatory-only result may already have fixed how the remaining tests read, and I have not seen it, so my bounds are wide on both information gain and rigor. The realized effect size is the main unknown.
